Act four. The auditor walks in and asks: can you prove it? What did the agent do, who let it, and how do you know?

Source: Ch 14

KASPER

First, what counts as evidence. On the left, a log line: what one program said at one moment. Fine for debugging, thin for an auditor.

On the right, what an auditor asks. What was decided, under which rule, at which limit, who asked, was a human involved, what reached the ledger. Each answer is one span field.

Source: Ch 3, Ch 9

KASPER

Before we look at the evidence, one honest question: when something gets refused, can you find the refusal later? We just saw four kinds of no. Here's which ones leave a trace, a recorded trail you can search afterwards.

1. Core, identity. A call with no valid token gets a 401 from agentgateway. Yes: the gateway writes a span with the 401 and the reason, JwtAuth. Layer two on the eight-layer slide.
2. Ring 1, reach. The Cilium drop from step 1. No. The packet is thrown away before any program sees it, so nothing writes a span. Cilium's flow viewer, Hubble, would record it, and we haven't installed it. A drop leaves no span.
3. Ring 2, capability. The policy service's deny. Yes, and the best case: it's inside the claim's own trace, as northstar.policy.decision, next to everything else the agent did.
4. The keystone. Kyverno's denial from step 4. Yes, but on its own. Kyverno sends its own trace, under the service kyverno-admission-controller: about eight spans, all under a millisecond, with the identity that asked and allowed equals false. It isn't joined to any agent's trace, because kubectl doesn't send a traceparent, the header that would link them. And we don't sample it: every denial is kept.

SAY: "So: traced everywhere except where a packet is dropped. That's a real gap, and I'd rather name it than hide it."

IF ASKED where the policy name is in Kyverno's span: only in the result message and in the webhook's URL path, /vpol/ plus the policy name. There's no dedicated attribute for it.

Source: M7 Kyverno trace findings (2026-10-12: service kyverno-admission-controller, admission.response.allowed=false, admission.request.user.name, admission.request.roles, no sampler); scripts/demo guard (Cilium drops are not in the trace; Hubble is not installed); the eight-layer slide (gateway 401 span, reason=JwtAuth)

KASPER

This is the evidence for one approval, straight from Jaeger. It's the second trace of a claim that waited for a person: it starts at the reviewer's decision.

Read the tags. The decision: approve. Who: the reviewer's id, and the reviewer service's own SPIFFE identity, so you know which workload signed, not just which name was typed. How long the human took: northstar.review.wait.duration, in seconds. And at the bottom, one reference: a link to a span in another trace. That's trace A, the agent's work, which ended when it handed the payment to a person.

SAY: "No new application code behind this. These are spans the system already emits. The evidence is the telemetry."

Captured 2026-10-19 from the M10 gate run's cluster; the claim id is a test claim.

One rule makes this view trustworthy: never sample the decision spans. Sample other traffic if you must; a missing decision looks exactly like one that never happened.

Source: Ch 9; M10 design spec (trace B and the resume link)

KASPER

From the evidence view to the thing it stands on. Left: a few lines of the schema, copied from telemetry/registry/policy.yaml in the repo, shortened only where you see the dots. It says that a policy decision is a server span called northstar.policy.decision, and that two attributes are required on it: the decision itself and the rule that fired. The limit is required only when the rule has one.

Right: Jaeger, the same span, on a real denied claim. Same names. Decision deny, rule settlement-agent.assisted.execute_limit, limit 0, requested 5800.

SAY: "Every name here starts with northstar dot. We did not make them up as we went: they are defined in a schema, and a checker called Weaver compares the running cluster against that schema."

Be plain about what the checker does not do (runbook §8, the contract): it does not catch a missing required attribute, and it does not judge span names. The behaviour tests pin those. Names from the OpenTelemetry conventions are not validated, only ours.

This slide sits outside the five-minute live block; cut it first if you are short.

Source: telemetry/registry/policy.yaml; docs/telemetry-contract.md "What live-check checks, and what it does not"; M9 Task 4

KASPER

One more word: evaluation. A grade, kept with the work it grades.

OpenTelemetry gives it four fields. A name: which check. A score: a number to graph. A label: pass or fail, to alert on. An explanation: why. The grade hangs off the span it judges.

Source: Ch 3

KASPER

So who checks the agent afterwards? Here, a small service called eval-scorer. Think of it as the auditor that never sleeps. Follow the four steps.

One: spans land. Every service sends its telemetry to the OpenTelemetry Collector, and the Collector keeps a copy in OpenSearch, the same spans Jaeger gets. Nothing extra is emitted for the scorer.

Two: read back. You ask it about one claim, POST slash score. It pulls every span of every trace that claim touched. If the read-back is cut short, it refuses to score. A trajectory with a missing piece always looks more compliant than it was: a retry that fell off the page is a retry it would never see.

Three: five checks, plain code, no model. Did the agent propose before it executed? Did it stop when it was refused? Did it record the refusal? Does the amount paid match the amount proposed and approved? Did the identity that paid have the authority? For that last one it keeps its own copy of the limits, so it can disagree with the policy service.

Four: written back. Each score goes out as an OpenTelemetry span, using the gen_ai.evaluation names you just saw, through the same Collector, parented to a real span in the trace it judged. Open the claim in Jaeger, and its grades are in the waterfall.

SAY: "OpenTelemetry in, OpenTelemetry out." The scores are telemetry like everything else, so any backend that reads OTLP can see them.

How it's emitted: OpenSearch's GenAI observability SDK (opensearch-genai-observability-sdk-py 0.2.8), its score() call. It writes a span named "evaluation <name>" plus a gen_ai.evaluation.result span event, per the GenAI conventions. The five checks themselves are ours: they are our policy, like the rules in the decision service.

IF ASKED "is that the standard shape?": close, not exact. The four attribute names match the convention. The convention's primary form is a log event, gen_ai.evaluation.result, parented to the operation it judged; we write a span plus a span event, because only a span can carry a link to the approval trace. The span's operation name "evaluation" is the OpenSearch SDK's own value, not a registered one (upstream PR #185 closed unmerged). Next step: add the log event and anchor scores on the agent's invoke_agent span.

Source: platform/eval-scorer/README.md; scorer/emit.py; scorer/opensearch.py (TrajectoryTruncated); scorer/authority.py; M4 design spec §5

eval-scorer is our auditor: plain code that reads a payment's spans back and scores five policy rules. This one asks: after a refusal, did the agent stop? A compliant run scores 1.0. KASPER

The usual answer is an LLM-as-judge: a second model reads the prompt, the tool calls and the answer, and grades the work. That answers "was it good?". An auditor asks "did it follow policy?".

Driving examiner versus speed camera: the camera just checks the number. Northstar has no LLM judge anywhere. Its scorer is deterministic and pull-only: it scores when asked. Both write the same gen_ai.evaluation fields, so a judge can come later.

IF ASKED "which judge?": two open-source options read the same OpenTelemetry GenAI traces. OpenLIT (Apache 2.0) runs LLM-as-judge and programmatic evals on production traces and has SDK guardrails. OpenSearch Agent Health compares an agent's trajectory with a "golden path", using an LLM judge. eval-scorer already emits through OpenSearch's GenAI observability SDK, the same family as Agent Health. Northstar has not run either one: say so.

[verify: OpenLIT and OpenSearch Agent Health feature lists at slide freeze (openlit.io; observability.opensearch.org/docs/agent-health)]

Source: Ch 3, Ch 9

KASPER

We wanted to know if an upstream tool could do this job, so we tried AgentEvals, from the kagent folks. Here's the most useful thing it taught us.

The setup: the agent was refused a payment, and then tried again, from a second trace. The check is "stopped when refused". It should fail.

Top row: AgentEvals, out of the box, grades one trace at a time. Trace A looks perfect: refused, stopped. The retry is in trace B, graded on its own. Result: pass. It missed it.

Middle row: same tool, but we give both traces the same claim id, so it grades them as one run. Now it fails. Caught.

Bottom row: our scorer follows the span link from one trace to the other, and it also sees the policy decision and who called. Fail, and it names the rule.

The lesson isn't "tool good, tool bad". A partial trajectory always reads higher. Whatever you grade with, group by the claim before you grade.

So that's what our demo does now: the settlement agent sends the claim id as the conversation id, and AgentEvals holds one session per claim. You saw it graded live, in the demo.

And the caveats, in the small print: the retry on this slide is staged, because our live agent never retried. And AgentEvals sees agent spans only, not the policy decision, not the human approval, not the caller's identity. One more thing we measured: its LLM judge isn't stable. The same claim scored 0.60, then 0.40, then 0.40 for hallucination, with nothing changed. That's why the checks on stage are deterministic code.

Source: AgentEvals trial 2026-10-21 (agentevals-cli 0.11.0, github.com/agentevals-dev): retry fixture, default grouping -> stopped_when_refused 1.0 PASS on both traces; with gen_ai.conversation.id=CLM-1842 on trace B and --group-by conversation -> 0.0 FAIL; eval-scorer scores.py stopped_when_refused (retry-after-refusal); memory: a partial trajectory always reads higher (M4)

KASPER

Our scorer asks "did it follow policy?". Teams running models in production add two more kinds of check, on the model itself.

On the left, evals, after the answer: was it good, did it make something up, is it biased or toxic? Usually a second model grades the first. On the right, guardrails, before the answer goes anywhere: a prompt injection, a sensitive topic, an agent wandering off its job. Wherever they run, record the result as gen_ai.evaluation.result beside the trace it judged.

SAY, plainly: "Our model calls don't go through a guardrail today."

Upstream, today: OpenLIT judges one model call at a time. Agent Health scores runs it starts itself. AgentEvals reads the traces you already have and writes the result back in the standard shape, and it now runs in our demo, beside our scorer. But it sees only what the agent did: not the policy decision, not the human, not the caller. So the five policy checks stay ours.

KASPER

Content capture means putting the actual words into telemetry: what the model was told, what it said, the arguments it passed to tools. In healthcare or finance that's often the most sensitive data you hold, so the first thing a privacy team asks is: can we turn it off and still audit?

We ran the same claim twice, capture on and off, and compared. Left, kept: the decision, the rule, the limit, who asked and as which identity, who approved, what happened to the payment. All of it comes from the platform's own spans, not from the model's text. Right, lost: the model's own account of itself.

So privacy and audit don't fight, as long as the evidence lives in the platform. What you lose is the model's side of the why. In production, keep that content outside the trace, behind its own access control.

IF ASKED (the measured pair): gen_ai keys barely move, 28 to 25, but the text inside them goes: text and thinking content 8 of 8 to 0 of 5, tool-call arguments 3 of 3 to 0 of 3, the messages shrink from 1,599 to 657 characters. The evidence view and the reviewer page don't change.

Source: Ch 9 (Figure 9.5)

KASPER

The goal is the right spans, not more spans. Northstar taught us one more lesson. Our second backend, OpenSearch, quietly rejected the policy decision spans. Jaeger had 142 spans, OpenSearch 139. The missing three were exactly the decisions. Losing data looks exactly like sampling it. So never sample the decisions. A test asserts 100% capture, and a parity guard compares span IDs across both backends, like counting parcels at both ends of the belt.

We can produce the evidence. But what do the regulations actually ask for? William.

Source: Ch 9

WILLIAM

Remember the questions we started with, the ones a regulator asks. Here is what answers them.

Read across: the law, what it asks for, and the Northstar artifact that answers it. Magenta text means not there yet. None of this makes you compliant. It gives your compliance people something to point at.

Row one: the AI Act's right to explanation, plus the EU court's Dun and Bradstreet ruling: a person is owed "the procedure and principles actually applied". A model card is the car's manual. A decision span is the dashcam footage: rule, limit, amount, caller.

Row two: DORA, the EU's rulebook for financial IT, wants logs protected against tampering, and logging failures detected. The parity guard covers the second half. We have no tamper protection. Strong at producing the record, weak at keeping it, and keeping it is what your organisation already knows how to do.

Not legal advice.

WILLIAM

Most 2025 talks said the AI Act's high-risk rules would bite on 2 August 2026, the struck-through date. They didn't. The Digital Omnibus, Regulation 2026/1744, moved Annex III to 2 December 2027. But record-keeping, oversight and explanation were not rewritten. The exam got postponed; the syllabus stayed. And in US banking, SR 26-2 replaced SR 11-7 in April and put generative and agentic AI out of scope, so platform controls fill that vacuum.

WILLIAM

So where does the industry stand? Here is a ladder for AI observability. Read it left to right, one rung at a time.

L0 is prompt logs: what was asked and answered, with a timestamp. L1 is model telemetry: model, latency, tokens, cost. L2 is connected traces: tools, retrieval and orchestration in one story. L3 is quality: evaluations and feedback. L4 is evaluation running all the time. And L5, top right, is governed agent observability: identity, permissions, trajectories, MCP, privacy controls.

Kasper's team measured seven ways to instrument the same agent. All seven reach L1. Three of seven reach L2. L3 is just starting, and nothing measured reached L4 or L5.

L5 is what this talk has been about. Everything you saw in Northstar is a piece of it. Like a building site: the ground floor is solid, the top floor is still scaffolding.

Source: Instrumenting AI Agents (Dash0 DevRel, Aug 2026), p. 10
